*Śivajñānasiddhi-svapakṣa-dṛṣṭāntasaṃgrahaḥ*.
Salutations to that Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing desired goals, and who cuts asunder all obstacles.
I bow to the elephant-faced one, white as a jasmine flower or the moon, who has destroyed his obstacles with his tusks;
he is accompanied by the song of bees falling upon the stream of his ichor.
I worship Śiva, who performs the eternal dance of bliss together with Umā in the midst of his glorious, cloud-like assembly, and who is served by all.
I bow to the Lord Śrī Nandikeśvara, who stands at the side of the gateway of Kailāsa, who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, and who is the beloved of Suyaśā.
A disciple of that teacher— who was a knower of truth and a perfect illuminator of awakening— named Aruṇandi, composed this authoritative treatise on the Āśā.
He composed three hundred [verses] known as the *Parapakṣāvabodha*;
there are five verses in the *Upodghāta* and fourteen in the *Pramāṇa*.
In the first [section] there are seventy verses; in the second, ninety-six;
and in the third as well, forty-four; in the fourth.
In the fifth [section] there is a group of nine; thereafter, that same number in the sixth sūtra;
but in the seventh there is a square of four, and likewise forty in the eighth.
In the ninth [chapter], twelve are declared; in the tenth, six are proclaimed;
in the eleventh, twelve; and in the twelfth, seven are recorded.
Then, after that, one's own side consists of three hundred and twenty-seven;
thus, with both sides combined, there are six hundred and twenty-seven.
Worshipping at the Guhāmaṭha in the meritorious Śrīmattillavana,
he became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Nigamajñāna.
The disciple who bore that name was the propagator of the tradition;
thus, having examined this scripture according to my understanding, [I have composed this].
For the sake of establishing its authority and for the renown of the root scripture,
he extracted passages from the Āgama scriptures and composed this supreme treatise.
Through the words of Svāyambhuva, satisfaction arises for the highest qualified practitioner; through the illustrative example alone, satisfaction arises for the middling qualified practitioner.
Whichever [system] may satisfy even the lowest qualified person—
whether it be Lokāyata, Buddhist, Ārhata, or Mīmāṃsā.
Māyāvāda and Pāñcarātra—these six are outside the [orthodox] systems (samaya). (From the Bhīmasaṃhitā, p. 970)

This knowledge should be bestowed [only upon the worthy]; one should not cause it to be given to others.
The twelfth sūtra is complete.

Thus ends the illustration from the *Śivajñānasiddhi*, which constitutes the essence of all the Āgamas, compiled by Vedajñānaśivācārya, the disciple of the illustrious Śivayogī Vedajñāna who resided in Vyāghrapura.
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Aruṇācala.
